title: Sunshine State
full_review:
Writer-director John Sayles tackles racism, developers, historical pageants and tourism in the flawed yet moving drama "Sunshine State" (Sony Classics).

The film is set on Plantation Island, Fla., where greedy real estate developers are looking to gobble up as much beachfront property as they can to build up the quiet beachside community into a hot spot for winter-weary northerners. Throughout the character and conversation-driven drama, change is the most constant aspect. Sayles layers the film with many personalities and story lines but focuses mainly on two very different women.

Having lived all her life on Plantation Island's Delrona Beach, Marly Temple (Edie Falco) is stuck running her father's seaside motel, which he had worked his fingers to the bone to see succeed. Too sick to manage the motel himself anymore, her nearly blind and very ornery, father Furman (Ralph Waite) sits at home spouting his opinions. Through him, Sayles relates the history of the island, but the history as seen from a white man's perspective.

Marly, divorced and with few aspirations, spends her time nursing hangovers and avoiding her ex-husband, leaving as much of the motel managing as she can to her workers. She is caught by surprise when romance begins to bloom with newcomer to town, Jack Meadows (Timothy Hutton), a landscape architect recently arrived to transform a section of the island into a "natural" gated community. As the boredom and monotony of her tired life continue to wear on her, Marly is tempted to give in to the strip mall developer who has offered to buy the motel.

In the next town over, Desiree Perry (Angela Bassett) returns home for the first time in 25 years to show off her anesthesiologist husband, Reggie (James McDaniel). Sent away by her proud parents at age 15 for having disgraced them by getting pregnant, Desiree is still intimidated by her strong-willed mother Eunice (Mary Alice). Like Marly's area, Desiree's small town of Lincoln Beach, an African-American enclave created during the era of segregation, has also become a target for developers.

Sayles fleshes out these two stories side by side, providing Desiree's with a historical voice in the form of Dr. Lloyd (Bill Cobbs), a moral man with a mission, who talks about the glory days of Lincoln Beach and fights to preserve it from real estate developers who care nothing about the people or their stories.

Throughout the film, Sayles inserts several seemingly disparate characters that initially have no apparent connection to each other or to Marly and Desiree. These subplots are not neatly developed, which seems purposeful. Sayles uses his supporting cast instead as dressing to depict the local color. He gives his movie a timeframe, unfolding the story during the weeklong Buccaneer Days Festival, a new "tradition" created by the local chamber of commerce headed by Francine Pickney (Mary Steenburgen). At a leisurely pace, the viewer soaks up the atmosphere and the slice of life that Sayles offers.

However, the unhurried pace at which Sayles sets the film in motion may cause the viewer's mind to wander a bit, as the film sometimes sags under the weight of the talky narrative. Yet "Sunshine State" and its characters remain memorable.

Falco offers an impressive performance, capturing the laid-back, flip-flop-wearing attitude of Marly. Falco is natural and convincing as a trapped woman looking for any way out, yet too lazy to actually do anything. Although her role is underwritten, Bassett infuses Desiree with vulnerabilities, showing that her old wounds are still not fully healed. When Flash Phillips (Tom Wright), a former football star who -- like Lincoln Beach -- has fallen upon hard times, reappears, old feelings and hurts are stirred up in Desiree. Bassett keeps these just below the surface, letting the viewer watch as she struggles to maintain her tidy life in control.

Through different circumstances by the film's end, both women are left on their own, freed from their past and now contemplating the future with hope in their hearts. But before the film concludes, Sayles has confronted entrenched racism in a small corner of the world while still portraying his main characters in an achingly human way, stripping away their hard exterior to show their imperfections and strengths.

"Sunshine State" is not a film that wraps things up in a neat package for the moviegoer to take home. Yet it lingers in the mind -� blemishes and all -� as a frieze about lonely people trying to make connections.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, an attempted suicide and some crass language and profanity with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III-adults. The Motion picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
